description: I’m Tanish, a Master of ICT student in Melbourne with a networking and cyber security background. I’m tackling the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge: a web app that merges two satellite fire-detection records into one burning-activity calendar, helping emergency responders and land managers explore historical fire patterns and critical periods. My focus is database design, data harmonization and backend development. I’m working solo.
summary: Sunza combines NASA MODIS (2000-) and VIIRS (2012-) active-fire hotspot data to create a uniform burning-activity calendar for Victoria, Australia. Raw counts cannot be compared between the 2012 boundary because the two sensors have different pixel sizes (1 km vs 375 m). They are calibrated during their overlapping time period (167 months, R² = 0.94) and the "VIIRS-equivalent" detections are calculated from MODIS counts, with one VIRISEQ detection using MODIS observations from 2000 to 2025. Aggregations are done at 0.1° grid cell and daily totals. All days are scored against the same time of year in all years and unusual days are also identified. The Web App displays a yearly-by-day heatmap, a map of burned areas, a list of the largest unusual periods and allows users to select a region or create an area of interest themselves. It enables emergency response, scientists and land managers to visualize historical fire patterns, critical periods and unusual conditions such as the Black Summer seasons of 2003, 2006-07, 2009 and 2019-20.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Sunza makes 25 years of satellite fire detection into one burning-activity calendar. Users pick a region (Whole state, Gippsland, North East Alps, Grampians, Otways) or draw any area on the map. They can view: (1) a year-by-day heat map: darker cells indicate more detections; (2) blue flags on days that are unusual for that time of year; (3) a map of the total activity in each cell (approx. 11 km) for a selected day, year or unusual period; and (4) a ranked list of the largest unusual periods.

HOW IT WORKS
1. ingest: MODIS and VIIRS hotspots from NASA FIRMS normalized to one schema (confidence normalized to low/nominal/high, size of the pixel per sensor).
2. Grid: Daily counts and FRP per 0.1° cell are aggregated for detection.
3. Calibrate: During the period of overlap (February 2012 onwards) least squares fitting was used to determine the relationship between VIIRS and MODIS based on monthly regional totals, for this purpose the coefficient k was determined. Detection counts: k = 5.43, R² = 0.94. Fire radiative power: k = 0.81, R² = 0.95 (167 months).
4. Harmonize: Values from VIIRS are used in locations where VIIRS is available, and MODIS x k are used before 20 Jan 2012. This provides a single source of VIIRS-equivalent detections.
5. Anomalies: each day's activity is compared to the average and standard deviation of the same time of year (+/- 7 days) for all years. All days with z >= 2 are flagged (user defined sensitivity).
The web front end (Leaflet) displays the calendar and map data that is computed on the fly by a backend (FastAPI).

IMPACT
The lack of a consistent view of when and where the fires occurred by fire managers is due to the distribution of the record amongst sensors. Sunza provides one comparable history to responders, scientists and land managers to help catch unusual conditions as early as possible, provide a glimpse into patterns for any area of interest, and pinpoint critical periods. The known major seasons (2003, 2006-07, 2009, 2019-20) stand out clearly, which supports the calibration.

TOOLS
Python, Pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Leaflet, OpenStreetMap tiles, HTML/CSS/JavaScript.

Two factors are considered. Two factors are taken into account:
We used a cell-centre rule for area selection, nominal + high confidence detections only, and a circular day-of-year baseline to ensure that the days in late-December and early-January compare correctly. Restrictions: regional calibration, different overpass for sensors, area filter is a bounding box.
